title: Table manners in different countries
examples: Why do people eat with their right hand in India?
What are table manners in different countries?

explain.say: Here is a puzzle: in one country, slurping your noodles is rude, and in another it says, this is delicious! Look at the board. In Japan, slurping noodles is okay, and you say itadakimasu before eating, a way of giving thanks.

But in Japan, never stand chopsticks upright in your rice, because that is done at funerals. Now look at India: many people eat with the right hand, after washing their hands. Have you eaten with your hands?

In Ethiopia, families share one big platter and scoop food with injera, a soft, spongy bread. Gursha means feeding a bite to someone you love. Look at the UK group: chew with your mouth closed and wait for everyone. Which surprised you?
So what if you visit a friend from another culture? Easy: watch the host and copy them, try a little of the new food, and ask if you are unsure, like, how do I eat this? Hosts love being asked.

faq.a: No. Slurping noodles like ramen or soba is normal in Japan and can show you are enjoying them. In many other countries, though, it can seem rude.

faq.q: Why do people eat with their right hand in India?
faq.a: In India and many other places, the right hand is used for eating and greeting, and the left for washing, so eating with the right hand is seen as clean and polite.
In Ethiopia, gursha is when you feed a bite of food, wrapped in injera, into a friend's or family member's mouth. It is a sign of love and friendship.

faq.q: What should I do at a friend's home for dinner?
faq.a: Watch your hosts and copy them, try a little of everything, ask if you are not sure, and say thank you at the end.

faq.q: Why should chopsticks not stand up in rice?
faq.a: In Japan and China, chopsticks standing upright in a bowl of rice look like incense sticks at a funeral, so it is seen as unlucky and rude.
asks: Tell me about the Chopsticks not up

facts: In Japan, sticking chopsticks upright in rice is avoided because it resembles a funeral offering.
Injera, a spongy flatbread made from teff, is used as both plate and spoon in Ethiopian meals.
In Japan, people say "itadakimasu" before a meal to give thanks for the food.
